summary: This is a structured narrative literature review (through November 4, 2026) examining the hypothesis that extracranial venous obstruction causes salivary lymphatic stasis and Sjögren-like autoimmunity. It integrates a single patient's clinical record (MRI volumetry, serological findings, treatment responses) with published experimental and human observational evidence across vascular anatomy, CNS drainage, lymphatic physiology, and salivary autoimmunity. The review concludes that while individual components of the proposed mechanism have experimental support, the complete human sequence from venous obstruction to PSP/CA6/SSA/ANA-positive autoimmune exocrinopathy remains undemonstrated.

content_blocks.title: Executive Assessment and Review Scope
content_blocks.content: The review covers neuro-lymphatic physiology, vascular hemodynamics, and immunology. The central hypothesis is that extracranial venous obstruction leads to salivary lymphatic stasis and Sjögren-like autoimmunity. The executive assessment states the literature supports mechanically initiated salivary autoimmunity in animals but does NOT establish the complete human sequence. Three key supporting findings: (1) Human venous obstruction can cause lymphatic reflux and venous thrombosis can cause parotid swelling; (2) Experimental salivary duct obstruction can produce salivary-reactive autoantibodies; (3) Experimental lymphatic dysfunction can disturb immune tolerance and generate local autoreactive immune responses. Clinical update documents: repeated benefit from glycopyrrolate and botulinum toxin; MRI-reported parotid reductions of 27% right and 20% left; immune findings: Ro52, CA6 IgM, and PSP IgM positivity; strong-positive ANA ELISA with negative HEp-2 IFA; SSA index declined but remains positive. Search scope: PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PMC, covering brachiocephalic/aortosternal obstruction, venous hypertension, thoracic duct and cervical lymphatic drainage, glymphatic/CSF transport, parotid/salivary glands, lymphatic stasis, autoantibodies, duct ligation, and Botox volumetry. Structured narrative review, not exhaustive systematic review. Evidence categorized as human observation, animal experiment, computational modeling, or mechanistic inference.

content_blocks.title: Treatment and Investigation Timeline (Clinical Case)
content_blocks.content:
Chronological clinical events for the index patient:
- July–October 2025: ENT note quotes substantial Robinul (glycopyrrolate) benefit at July 24 visit; further benefit from right-parotid Botox by October 28. Symptom responses preceded the February 2026 guided procedure.
- November 12, 2025: ANA ELISA and antigen-specific antibody panel collected; reported November 17. Conventional immune findings present before February procedure and March MRI.
- December 10–15, 2025: Botox on December 10; comparison MRI acquired December 15 (5 days post-injection, not untreated baseline).
- December 23, 2025: Robinul use temporarily fell to 1 mg/day after Botox, then returned to 6 mg/day as symptoms partly recurred.
- February 4, 2026: Ultrasound-guided treatment of both parotid and both submandibular glands; 50 units each, 200 units total.
- March 16, 2026: Follow-up MRI reports parotid volume reductions of 27% right and 20% left, with near-symmetry. Structural response ~40 days after guided procedure.
- April 2026: Rheumatology assessed likely primary seropositive Sjögren disease with atypical sialorrhea, ESSDAI 0, no current parotid hypertrophy. Hydroxychloroquine and further evaluation proposed.
- July 28, 2026: 80-unit Xeomin (incobotulinumtoxin A) procedure; near-complete benefit from preceding treatment; glycopyrrolate stopped; hydroxychloroquine continued.
- September 9, 2026: Early salivary-antibody and differential-diagnosis panels collected; anti-CA6 IgM and anti-PSP IgM positive.
- October 28, 2026: Vascular-imaging correspondence requests assessment of localized jugular/lymphovenous and central outflow hypothesis; no completed pressure study or venous decompression documented.

content_blocks.title: MRI Parotid Gland Measurements
content_blocks.content:
Certified radiologist measurements from two MRI scans:

Right parotid:
- Comparison MRI (December 15, 2025): 26 mL; 3.0 x 3.0 x 5.8 cm
- Follow-up MRI (March 16, 2026): 19 mL; 2.8 x 2.7 x 5.0 cm
- Reported reduction: 27% (calculated: 26.9%)

Left parotid:
- Comparison MRI (December 15, 2025): 24 mL; 3.2 x 2.5 x 6.0 cm
- Follow-up MRI (March 16, 2026): 19 mL; 2.9 x 2.4 x 5.5 cm
- Reported reduction: 20% (calculated: 20.8%)

Caveats: Volumetric method not specified; MRI protocols differed; comparison MRI was 5 days after a prior injection; ongoing secretory treatment complicates attribution. Comparison report: slight right asymmetry, ~2 cm accessory right parotid focus in cheek, normal intraparotid nodes, no ductal dilatation, no salivary leak, normal occipital/retroauricular veins; sialadenosis/sialosis considered. Follow-up: smaller nearly symmetric parotids, normal symmetric Stensen ducts, unchanged accessory tissue, no pathological enhancement, no focal lesion, no ductal dilatation; submandibular and sublingual glands normal.

content_blocks.title: Immune Findings: November 2025 Panel (Connective Tissue Disease)
content_blocks.content:
Specimen collected November 12, 2025; reported November 17, 2025.

- ANA IgG, ELISA: >150 Units — Strong positive (threshold ≥60 Units)
- ANA, HEp-2 IFA: Negative — No nuclear or cytoplasmic pattern (positive threshold 1:80)
- Anti-SSA/Ro52 IgG, ELFA: 107.0 U/mL — Positive (threshold >10 U/mL)
- Anti-SSA/Ro60 IgG, ELFA: <0.4 U/mL — Negative (negative range <7 U/mL)
- Anti-SSB/La IgG, ELFA: <0.4 U/mL — Negative (negative range <7 U/mL)

Both positive ANA ELISA and negative ANA IFA confirmed by repeat testing. Case described as: strong-positive ANA by ELISA with repeat-confirmed negative HEp-2 IFA. ELFA = enzyme-linked fluorescent assay.

content_blocks.title: Immune Findings: September 2026 Early Salivary-Antibody Panel
content_blocks.content:
Specimen collected September 9, 2026; reported September 16, 2026. All nine measurements use ELISA, reported in EU/mL. Laboratory ranges: negative <20, borderline 20–25, positive >25.

Salivary protein 1 (SP1):
- IgG: 7.9 EU/mL — negative
- IgA: 3.4 EU/mL — negative
- IgM: 15.2 EU/mL — negative

Carbonic anhydrase VI (CA6):
- IgG: 6.0 EU/mL — negative
- IgA: 5.0 EU/mL — negative
- IgM: 29.4 EU/mL — POSITIVE

Parotid-specific protein (PSP):
- IgG: 13.6 EU/mL — negative
- IgA: 6.3 EU/mL — negative
- IgM: 36.0 EU/mL — POSITIVE

Two positive results: anti-CA6 IgM and anti-PSP IgM; seven negative. Differential context (same specimen date): ANCA negative by IIF; MPO and PR3 <1.0 AI; ACE 54 U/L (range 9–67); serum IgG4 63.8 mg/dL (range 4.0–86.0); Crithidia dsDNA IFA negative.

content_blocks.title: Anti-SSA Trend Analysis
content_blocks.content: Portal image shows anti-SSA values: 4.1, 1.9, 2.2, and 1.6 AI (one additional early point without readable label). Latest value 1.6 AI remains above 0.9 AI upper reference limit. History fluctuates rather than falling monotonically. Anti-SSB latest value below 0.2 AI. The main early fall appears before the 2025–2026 part of the displayed timeline, so it cannot be attributed to the February 2026 procedure. Ro52 107.0 U/mL, portal SSA in AI, and PSP/CA6 in EU/mL must not be combined into a single numerical trajectory. Reference: Praprotnik et al. (1999) prospective study of 15 Sjögren and 16 lupus patients found anti-Ro titers fluctuated over 2 years and usually did not parallel clinical activity.

content_blocks.title: Section 1: Venous Bottleneck and Salivary Lymphatic Drainage — Anatomy and Physiology
content_blocks.content:
Parotid lymphatic anatomy: Marchetti et al. (1989) identified lymphatic capillaries in connective septa and around striated ducts, with collecting vessels near larger excretory ducts. This interstitial drainage network is distinct from salivary ducts. Fluid drains through intraparotid/periparotid and cervical pathways to lymphovenous outlets in the lower neck. Not all head-and-neck lymph passes through the thoracic duct; left and right drainage territories vary.

Physiological 'pressure lock': Increased lymphatic outflow pressure is the key mechanism. Conceptual relationship: Qlymph ~ (Pupstream + ΔPlymphatic pump - Poutlet) / Reffective. Reduced forward flow does not automatically mean reverse flow — competent valves can produce stasis. Reflux requires specific pressure gradients and valvular conditions.

Key experimental evidence:
- Kim and Tithof (2024): Computational model of cervical lymphatic transport demonstrated near-stalling and small retrograde flows under adverse pressure conditions. Supports hydraulic plausibility but does not establish human diagnostic threshold or parotid reflux pathway.
- Brace and Valenzuela (1990): Directly varied thoracic-duct outlet pressure in 6 awake sheep. Flow fell once adverse outlet pressure was sufficiently high; complete cessation at 25.6 ± 4.2 mmHg. Demonstrates finite transport reserve and pressure-dependent limit, not inevitable failure with every venous pressure rise. Not a human diagnostic threshold; did not measure parotid drainage.

content_blocks.title: Human Evidence: Venous Obstruction Producing Upstream Effects
content_blocks.content:
Study | Observation | What it establishes

Giglio et al. (2022) — aortosternal venous compression: Dynamic left brachiocephalic narrowing, including expiratory obstruction and cephalad contrast reflux into left internal jugular vein. → Aortosternal compression can be hemodynamically consequential; demonstrated reflux was venous, not glandular lymphatic.

Herzig et al. (2013) — brachiocephalic stenosis: Two patients with dialysis fistulas developed intracranial venous congestion and neurological complications, with improvement after addressing abnormal outflow/high-flow circuit. → Extracranial venous disease can affect intracranial hemodynamics; high-flow dialysis setting limits generalization.

Kaur et al. (2026) — pacemaker-related obstruction: Venous stenosis accompanied thoracic duct dilation and mesenteric lymphatic reflux; definitive treatment of venous problem resolved chylous ascites. → Direct clinical evidence that venous obstruction can generate pathological lymphatic reflux, demonstrated in abdominal drainage territory.

Mestre & Gil (2024) — catheter-related thrombosis: External jugular thrombosis associated with parotid swelling, resolving after catheter removal and anticoagulation. → Venous obstruction can cause salivary-region swelling phenotype without establishing autoimmune disease.

None of these reports demonstrates the entire proposed sequence.

content_blocks.title: Section 2: Intracranial Compartment Physiology and Proposed CNS-to-Parotid Route
content_blocks.content:
Intracranial compartmental syndrome framework (Godoy et al. 2023; Brasil et al. 2025 — Monro-Kellie 4.0): Provides framework for impaired venous and fluid outflow but does NOT establish a validated chronic 'glymphatic pressure lock' syndrome causing parotid autoimmunity. Glymphatic exchange within/around brain tissue is distinct from extracranial lymphatic efflux.

Key experiments:
- Hussain et al. (2023): Mouse TBI model — adrenergic surge associated with elevated central venous pressure and impaired cervical lymphatic transport. Adrenergic inhibition improved drainage and reduced cerebral edema. Not an isolated test of brachiocephalic obstruction.
- Xiang et al. (2022): Experimentally raised ICP → impaired glymphatic influx and cervical lymphatic efflux, alongside increased drainage through spinal/sacral routes. Demonstrates pressure disturbance redistributes drainage rather than uniform shutdown. Did not show diversion into salivary parenchyma.
- El Kamouh et al. (2026): Bilateral internal and external jugular vein ligation in adult female mice. ICP rose at day 2, normalized by day 7; brain enlargement resolved by day 60. Dorsal meningeal lymphatics regressed then recovered. VEGF-C trap raised pressure and prevented normal recovery. Cervical-node tracer kinetics accelerated during compensation (not uniform downstream stasis). Human comparison: 16 women with idiopathic intracranial hypertension vs. 19 healthy women — altered perisinusal enhancement with venous stenoses (indirect surrogate; BMI and acetazolamide use limit interpretation). Did not examine parotid reflux, salivary injury, or autoantibodies.

CNS-to-parotid region evidence:
1. Eide et al. (2018): Intrathecal MRI tracer in 19 humans → transport to cervical lymph nodes. Supports CSF-to-cervical drainage connection; does NOT establish entry into salivary acini or ducts.
2. Sigurdsson et al. (2023): CSF tracer detected in region containing superficial parotid AND deep cervical lymph nodes in rats; imaging could not separate structures due to proximity/resolution. Supports regional nodal drainage, not proof of tracer entering salivary gland itself.
3. Jin et al. (2025): Mapped multiple cranial drainage routes into cervical nodes in mice. Most configurations did not show visible parotid-node tracer; anatomical variant (fusion of accessory submandibular and parotid nodes) permitted labeling of adjacent parotid portion. Two macaques: tracer reached submandibular/retropharyngeal nodes without demonstrated parotid labeling.
4. Nguyen et al. (2026): Human cadaver mapping of cranial lymphatic pathways toward level II cervical nodes; β-amyloid staining in cervical nodes from dementia cadaver. Cadaver observations cannot establish living flow direction.

Critical distinction: parotid lymph node ≠ parotid secretory tissue. CNS material reaching a node near a gland does not demonstrate exposure of acinar cells, ductal cells, or glandular interstitium.

content_blocks.title: Section 3: Experimental Evidence — Mechanical Obstruction/Lymphatic Stasis Initiating Autoimmunity
content_blocks.content:
Study | Experimental finding | Relevance and limitation

Ohno et al. (2007) — salivary duct ligation: Unilateral submandibular duct ligation in 5 mouse strains → local inflammation/atrophy; 3 strains developed salivary-reactive autoantibodies; 2 developed inflammation in opposite unligated gland. → Closest direct precedent for mechanically initiated salivary autoreactivity, with genetic dependence. Was salivary duct obstruction, not lymphatic/venous obstruction. Antibodies not identified as PSP, CA6, SSA, or ANA.

Thomas et al. (2012) — absent dermal lymphatic drainage: K14-VEGFR-3-Ig mice showed impaired antigen/cell transport and disturbed tolerance; aged animals developed autoreactivity including anti-dsDNA. → Demonstrates defective lymphatic drainage can coexist with loss of tolerance. Developmental skin lymphatic deficiency ≠ acquired cervical congestion.

Summers et al. (2025) — lung lymphatic dysfunction: CLEC2-deficient mice developed organized lung immune aggregates producing local anti-elastin and anti-collagen antibodies. Anti-CD20 treatment reduced aggregate formation and partially prevented emphysema. → Strong evidence connecting lymphatic dysfunction with local, pathogenic autoreactive immunity. Antibodies increased in lung lavage rather than serum; model does not establish salivary disease.

Campbell et al. (2025) — human lymphedema: Paired affected/unaffected skin from 11 breast cancer-related lymphedema patients showed antigen-driven CD4 T-cell expansion with evidence implicating self-antigen responses. → Human evidence that chronic lymphatic disease can involve antigen-specific immunity. Does not establish Sjögren antibodies or isolate congestion from treatment-related tissue injury.

Howlader et al. (2025) — lupus and lymphatic function: Improving lymphatic drainage in lupus-prone mice reduced cutaneous inflammation and altered lymph-node immune responses. Some autoantibody responses declined; anti-DNA and RNP did not show same reduction. → Supports lymphatic function as immune modifier; argues against assuming all autoantibodies track fluid clearance uniformly.

Nakamura et al. (2021) — salivary epithelial injury: Local LAMP3 overexpression in mouse salivary glands → hyposecretion, inflammatory infiltration, and anti-SSA/SSB production over time. → Demonstrates gland-intrinsic perturbation can precede characteristic autoimmunity. Initiating intervention was genetic; congestion-to-LAMP3 pathway not tested.

Cohen et al. (2010): Lymph-node lymphatic endothelial cells can present self-antigen and delete responding CD8 T cells → lymphatic dysfunction could affect autoimmunity through immune regulation beyond simple protein removal.

content_blocks.title: Section 3: Proposed Biologically Coherent Working Sequence
content_blocks.content:
Proposed 5-step mechanistic sequence (each step has experimental support in isolation; operation as continuous pathway in venously congested human parotid remains inference):
1. Impaired outflow prolongs interstitial retention and changes local mechanical and inflammatory environment.
2. Epithelial stress or injury releases self-antigens and danger signals.
3. Altered lymphatic transport changes antigen presentation and immune-cell trafficking.
4. In a susceptible host, autoreactive T- and B-cell responses expand.
5. Persistent inflammation and structural remodeling could further impair drainage, creating a feedback loop.

Key implication: CNS-derived proteins are NOT necessary for the mechanically initiated autoimmune hypothesis. Injured salivary tissue already supplies relevant self-antigens. CNS cargo would constitute an additional proposed trigger or amplifier requiring its own evidence.

content_blocks.title: Section 4: Evidence Assessment for PSP, CA6, Anti-SSA, and ANA
content_blocks.content:
Marker | What the evidence supports | What it cannot currently establish

Anti-PSP: Autoreactivity to a salivary-associated protein; reported across Sjögren and comparison populations. | That lymphatic retention caused the antibody, or that the initiating material came from the CNS.

Anti-CA6: Another salivary-associated autoreactivity with limited disease specificity in current validation data. | A congestion-specific mechanism, or disease timing from antibody positivity alone.

Anti-SSA/Ro: Established and clinically important Sjögren-associated marker; salivary epithelial perturbation can generate it in animal model. | Whether the initiating event was vascular, epithelial, infectious, or another immune process.

Strongly positive ANA: Evidence requiring interpretation by titer, pattern, assay, and clinical context. | The anatomical origin of immune activation, or proof that glandular congestion caused systemic autoimmunity.

Key validation data: Johr et al. (2026) analyzed 444 participants (149 Sjögren, comparison groups with other autoimmune diseases, nonspecific chronic sialadenitis, controls). Serum PSP/CA6/SP1 positivity did not differ meaningfully across diagnostic groups; any-positive serum panel AUC = 0.47; positive likelihood ratio 1.04 against chronic sialadenitis (essentially no discrimination). Some salivary measurements performed differently from serum measurements.

Ro52/Ro60 distinction: Armağan et al. (2022) — 58/390 participants meeting Sjögren classification criteria had isolated anti-Ro52; 58/95 with isolated anti-Ro52 in full referral cohort fulfilled criteria. Pattern can occur in genuine Sjögren disease but antibody alone did not establish classification.

Temporal caveat: Theander et al. (2015) detected Sjögren-associated autoantibodies years (sometimes ~2 decades) before clinical diagnosis. A first positive test after swelling or venous symptoms does not establish when immune response began.

No study identified demonstrating that measured salivary lymphatic stasis subsequently causes the combined PSP/CA6/anti-SSA/strongly positive ANA profile in humans.

content_blocks.title: Section 5: Botulinum Toxin — Reduced Secretion and Gland Volume
content_blocks.content:
Mechanism of Botox on salivary glands:
- Xu et al. (2015): Pre- and postsynaptic effects including reduced secretion and altered AQP5 distribution.
- Teymoortash et al. (2007): Structural and functional changes in rat acinar cells including atrophy and reduced secretory granules.
- A smaller gland after treatment can reflect reduced secretory activity and tissue remodeling, not necessarily removal of accumulated lymph.

MRI reduction (27% right, 20% left): Documented bilateral size change. Jeong et al. (2024) RCT (30 enrolled, 27 completed) demonstrated volumetric effect of botulinum toxin type A on parotid gland. Volume reduction cannot be converted to pressure reduction without knowing gland compliance, vascular/interstitial fluid content, and contribution of cellular atrophy.

Four pressure compartments that must be separated:
1. Salivary duct lumen: Lower secretion can reduce flow-related duct loading.
2. Gland interstitium: Net effect uncertain — secretion changes both fluid delivery and epithelial fluid extraction.
3. Lymphatic collectors: Reduced local fluid load might help, but direct improvement in salivary lymphatic pumping/clearance not demonstrated.
4. Regional veins: Parotid injection does not remove the central venous lesion.

Counterintuitive finding: Berggreen and Wiig (2006) — stimulating secretion in rat submandibular glands LOWERED interstitial pressure by ~3.8 mmHg from resting value of ~+3 mmHg. Challenges simple assumption that greater secretion raises surrounding tissue pressure.

Smaje and Gamble (1987): Stimulation in rabbit glands markedly increased blood flow and interstitial fluid production — secretion involves substantial vascular recruitment.

Conceptual balance: dVinterstitium/dt = Jvascular filtration - Qlymphatic clearance - Jepithelial fluid extraction. Net effect on edema cannot be inferred from saliva suppression alone.

Kwon et al. (2021): Prospective multicenter study of 14 chronic parotitis patients — symptomatic improvement WITHOUT statistically significant change in whole-gland volume or measured salivary function.

O'Neil et al. (2016): Botox relieved recurrent parotitis in established Sjögren syndrome patient — response does not distinguish mechanical from autoimmune disease.

content_blocks.title: Section 6: Rheumatology Assessment Gaps and Unresolved Questions
content_blocks.content:
Rheumatology assessment (April 2026): Recognized atypical sialorrhea, significant but temporary Botox benefit, glycopyrrolate benefit, dry eyes developing after secretion-suppressing treatment. Recorded likely primary seropositive Sjögren disease, ESSDAI 0, no current parotid hypertrophy. Proposed hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day, repeat immune/renal studies, consideration of minor salivary-gland biopsy. No completed salivary biopsy, focus score, Schirmer/ocular-staining results, or quantified salivary flow in supplied note.

Four unresolved clinical questions:
1. Production vs. retention: Was 'sialorrhea' objectively shown to reflect excessive secretion, impaired handling/drainage, or combination?
2. Sicca attribution: What ocular and salivary findings persist when medication effects are appropriately accounted for?
3. Outflow physiology: Is there a functionally significant regional venous lesion, and does it impair the affected gland's lymphatic clearance?
4. Causal order: Did impaired outflow precede immune activation, did inflammation impair drainage, or do both coexist and reinforce one another?

ACR/EULAR criteria (Shiboski et al. 2017): Emphasize anti-SSA, focal lymphocytic sialadenitis, ocular findings, and salivary hypofunction. PSP, CA6, and ANA alone are not scoring items. Criteria do not adjudicate whether a vascular factor initiated or amplified disease.

Lymphatic appearance ≠ lymphatic function: Alunno et al. (2016) reported lymphatic neovascularization in Sjögren tissue; McCall and Baker (2015) did not find comparable changes. Neither vessel density nor static gland image establishes drainage direction, pressure, pumping, or clearance.

Sialendoscopy evidence: Karagozoglu et al. (2021) RCT — sialendoscopy improved salivary secretion and dryness outcomes for up to 60 weeks in Sjögren patients. Improvement after mechanical intervention does not invalidate autoimmune diagnosis.

Functional regional venous disease may escape static assessment: Respiratory variation in aortosternal compression illustrates that one imaging phase may inadequately characterize an intermittent lesion.

content_blocks.title: Section 7: What Would Demonstrate the Complete Mechanism
content_blocks.content:
Links requiring demonstration and most informative evidence:

1. The venous lesion is functionally important → Pressure and flow measurements across the lesion, accounting for respiration, posture, and collateral drainage.

2. It impairs the relevant gland's lymphatic outflow → Directional lymphatic imaging or validated clearance measurements matched to the affected gland and side.

3. CNS-derived material reaches salivary tissue → Tracer or molecular evidence localized to glandular interstitium/acini/ducts, separated from nearby lymph nodes and blood-borne delivery.

4. Congestion precedes immune activation → Longitudinal samples showing ordering of obstruction, tissue injury, local immune changes, and antibody emergence.

5. The immune response targets relevant antigens → Tissue-level antigen identification, autoreactive cell characterization, and corresponding serum/salivary antibody measurements.

6. Correcting outflow modifies the pathway → Before-and-after studies of clinically indicated outflow treatment, measuring lymph clearance, gland function, tissue inflammation, and immune endpoints separately.

7. Botox relieves lymphatic loading specifically → Demonstrated changes in lymphatic clearance or interstitial pressure, beyond reduced secretion, pain, or gland size.

Appropriate comparison groups: conventional Sjögren without identified obstruction, obstruction without autoimmune features, chronic ductal sialadenitis, and controls. Antibody persistence after decompression would need cautious interpretation.

content_blocks.title: Figure 1: Simplified Regional Drainage Map
content_blocks.content:
Diagram showing two parallel drainage pathways converging at cervical lymphatic trunks:
- Left pathway: CNS fluid and solutes → Cranial exit routes and cervical lymphatics → Cervical lymphatic trunks
- Right pathway: Parotid interstitial fluid → Parotid nodes and cervical collectors → Cervical lymphatic trunks
- Both converge: Cervical lymphatic trunks → Lymphovenous outlets → Central venous circulation
- Dotted arrow (labeled 'Proposed reflux / Unverified in gland tissue') shows hypothetical retrograde flow from cervical lymphatic trunks back to parotid interstitial fluid

Solid arrows indicate usual forward routes. The dotted arrow represents the proposed, unverified reflux into gland tissue. Individual anatomical connections vary. Diagram represents regional convergence, not a single shared pipe.

key_findings: The literature supports mechanically initiated salivary autoimmunity in animals (Ohno et al. 2007: unilateral submandibular duct ligation in mice produced salivary-reactive autoantibodies in 3 of 5 strains) but does NOT establish the complete human sequence from extracranial venous obstruction to PSP/CA6/SSA/ANA-positive autoimmune exocrinopathy.
Clinical case: MRI-documented bilateral parotid volume reduction of 27% right (26→19 mL) and 20% left (24→19 mL) between December 15, 2025 and March 16, 2026, following botulinum toxin treatment.

Clinical case immune profile: Strong-positive ANA ELISA (>150 Units; threshold ≥60) with repeat-confirmed negative HEp-2 IFA; Anti-SSA/Ro52 IgG 107.0 U/mL (positive); Anti-SSA/Ro60 and Anti-SSB/La negative; Anti-CA6 IgM 29.4 EU/mL (positive); Anti-PSP IgM 36.0 EU/mL (positive); SP1 all isotypes negative.

Johr et al. (2026) validation study (n=444, including 149 Sjögren): Serum PSP/CA6/SP1 positivity did not differ meaningfully across diagnostic groups; any-positive serum panel AUC = 0.47; positive likelihood ratio 1.04 against chronic sialadenitis — essentially no diagnostic discrimination.

Kaur et al. (2026): Direct clinical evidence that venous obstruction (pacemaker-related) caused thoracic duct dilation and mesenteric lymphatic reflux; treatment of venous problem resolved chylous ascites.

Mestre & Gil (2024): External jugular thrombosis associated with parotid swelling, resolving after catheter removal and anticoagulation — venous obstruction can cause salivary-region swelling without autoimmune disease.

El Kamouh et al. (2026): Bilateral jugular vein ligation in mice raised ICP at day 2 (normalized day 7); brain enlargement resolved by day 60; dorsal meningeal lymphatics regressed then recovered; VEGF-C trap prevented normal recovery. Human comparison: altered perisinusal enhancement in 16 women with idiopathic intracranial hypertension vs. 19 healthy controls.
Brace and Valenzuela (1990): Thoracic duct lymph flow cessation at 25.6 ± 4.2 mmHg adverse outlet pressure in 6 awake sheep — demonstrates finite transport reserve and pressure-dependent limit.

Kim and Tithof (2024): Computational model demonstrated near-stalling and small retrograde flows in cervical lymphatics under adverse pressure conditions — supports hydraulic plausibility of outflow failure.

Summers et al. (2025): CLEC2-deficient mice with lymphatic dysfunction developed organized lung immune aggregates producing local anti-elastin and anti-collagen antibodies — strong evidence connecting lymphatic dysfunction with local pathogenic autoreactive immunity.

Rheumatology assessment (April 2026): Likely primary seropositive Sjögren disease, ESSDAI 0, no current parotid hypertrophy; hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day proposed; no completed salivary biopsy or quantified salivary flow.

Anti-SSA trend (portal image): Values 4.1, 1.9, 2.2, 1.6 AI — declining but persistently above 0.9 AI upper reference limit; main early fall predates 2025–2026 timeline and cannot be attributed to February 2026 procedure.

Berggreen and Wiig (2006): Stimulating secretion in rat submandibular glands LOWERED interstitial pressure by ~3.8 mmHg — challenges assumption that greater secretion raises surrounding tissue pressure.
Theander et al. (2015): Sjögren-associated autoantibodies detectable years to ~2 decades before clinical diagnosis — first positive test after symptoms does not establish when immune response began.

No study identified demonstrating that measured salivary lymphatic stasis subsequently causes the combined PSP/CA6/anti-SSA/strongly positive ANA profile in humans — identified as a specific research gap.

Anti-CA6 IgM 29.4 EU/mL (positive) and anti-PSP IgM 36.0 EU/mL (positive). SP1 all isotypes negative. ANCA negative; MPO/PR3 <1.0 AI; ACE 54 U/L; IgG4 63.8 mg/dL; Crithidia dsDNA IFA negative.
milestones.source_quote: Early salivary-antibody and differential-diagnosis panels collected. Anti-CA6 IgM and anti-PSP IgM were positive. [I, J]

milestones.title: Vascular-imaging correspondence requesting outflow assessment
milestones.description: Clinician-researcher correspondence dated October 28, 2026 requests assessment of localized jugular/lymphovenous and central outflow hypothesis. Identifies suspicious region at base of right internal jugular vein near lymphovenous junction. No completed pressure study or venous decompression documented.
milestones.source_quote: Vascular-imaging correspondence requests assessment of a localized jugular/lymphovenous and central outflow hypothesis. [L]
